cases.title: Four regiments assigned, three equipped
cases.mission: The 14th Mixed Aviation Division reported 51 aircraft with the 17th Fighter Regiment, 55 with the 46th, 66 with the 89th and two at headquarters. The 253rd Assault Regiment had seven pilots and no aircraft. The 46th flew from the Mlynuv area on 22 June, where pilot Ivan Ivanov died.
cases.effect: On 23 June Fifth Army ordered the 14th and 62nd divisions to cover 22nd Mechanized Corps as it assembled. Southwestern Front subsequently acknowledged late support to ground troops and 237 aircraft destroyed or damaged on its own fields on 22–24 June.
cases.limit: Fifth Army calls the 14th a fighter division and the 62nd mixed. The front’s own organisational return calls them mixed and bomber respectively. The order identifies the intended beneficiary; it does not record completion or attribute the 237 front-wide losses to these divisions.

cases.title: What the northern German fighter return actually counted
cases.mission: All three Gruppen of JG 54 were deployed in Luftflotte 1. Together they reported 102 serviceable fighters out of 120. Separately, two JG 53 Staffeln attached to the northern force reported 33 serviceable out of 35 between them.
cases.effect: The return establishes a larger fighter force than the three JG 54 Gruppen alone. In the south, Romania fielded three fighter groups of its own for the Bessarabian front.
cases.limit: Neither deployment return assigns an opening-day Soviet loss or a completed escort to a particular German or Romanian squadron. The German and Romanian figures cover different sectors.

cases.title: What Romania’s fighter groups did before the pocket formed
cases.mission: On 9 September the 6th Group sent eight aircraft on two sector-reconnaissance missions. The 7th logged 36 aircraft appearances on nine fighter sweeps, the 8th logged 19 on six familiarisation missions. From 9–18 September the Romanian formation reported 524 fighter sorties, many escorting German bombers.
cases.effect: German dive-bomber crews praised the Romanian escort in a 15 September command order. This identifies the immediate beneficiary and a contemporary assessment of the cover.
cases.limit: The 524 sorties span several roles. No paired German bomber loss series or Soviet interception return establishes how many losses the escort prevented. Parent-group totals do not prove every assigned squadron flew that day.

cases.title: How many of the 26 Romanian squadrons can be named?
cases.mission: The air force counted 26 in seven roles at the end of September. German mission correspondence gives group sizes and equipment. Comparison with a dated September squadron register identifies 17 by role, including the 108th medical unit.
cases.effect: The 1 October command return distinguishes 17 combat-group squadrons, six observers serving the two Romanian armies and three transport or medical squadrons. This is a broader force than the fighters alone.
cases.limit: The two specialist chronologies disagree over when 5th Bomber Group arrived. They place 1st and 3rd Bomber Groups in October. All seven bomber identities are kept outside the 26. The sixth observer (14th or 17th) and second Ju 52 transport remain open.

cases.title: The transports that reached Sixth Army
cases.mission: On 29 November 38 Ju 52s and 21 He 111s took off. Twelve and thirteen, respectively, landed in the pocket. On 30 November the sources say 39 and 38 were committed, of which 30 and 36 landed.
cases.effect: The pocket received 25 aircraft landings from 59 take-offs on the 29th and 66 from 77 aircraft committed on the 30th. Richthofen’s diary separately records 75 tons delivered against a 300-ton order on 25 November.
cases.limit: Commitment and take-off are different dispatch measures. An arrival is neither an aircraft loss nor a weighed cargo receipt. Daily manifests for 29–30 November and Sixth Army’s distribution below the airfield remain open.

cases.title: Soviet fighter strength during Uranus
cases.mission: The 8th, 16th and 17th Air Armies appear in a three-row return with 284, 114 and 82 fighters. The sum is 480 fighters within 1,267 aircraft on strength across those rows.
cases.effect: It establishes the scale available to three commands during the counteroffensive. It also exposes a boundary: the 2nd Air Army could be operationally subordinated across the administrative front boundary.
cases.limit: Airframes on strength and pilots actually flying are different counts. These three rows cannot supply a sortie or casualty attribution.

cases.title: What the army quartermaster actually received
cases.mission: The Sixth Army quartermaster recorded 125 tons of incoming supplies on 16 December, about two-thirds fuel. His diary distinguished the fuel and ammunition position from the need for food, particularly bread.
cases.effect: The receiving army judged fuel and ammunition sufficient for the first operations it envisaged and asked for the cargo mix to change. Its account documents which need a delivery relieved and which need persisted.
cases.limit: The diary does not give the dispatched tonnage for this date or trace distribution to individual divisions. The November arrival fractions and the December receipt cannot be combined into a single delivery rate.

cases.title: Northern face: 1,232 sorties and an army still short of support
cases.mission: Eight fighters from the Soviet 53rd Guards Fighter Aviation Regiment engaged German bombers. The 54th Guards and 519th Fighter Regiments also appear in the first-day combat account. Across all roles, 16th Air Army recorded 1,232 sorties.
cases.effect: That army’s own history says ground troops received inadequate support and reports German penetration of 6–8 km on the main axis. The Central Front wartime order names both 2nd Tank Army and 16th Air Army for the counterattack.
cases.limit: The front order shows the intended cooperation. A particular regiment’s effect on the advance has not been isolated. The air army’s 106 aerial victories are claims without a matching German loss return.

cases.title: Southern face: two Soviet air armies struck together
cases.mission: Kozhevnikov groups 417 assault aircraft and fighters from 2nd and 17th Air Armies in the morning attacks on seven airfields. He also records support near the Seversky Donets crossings and names the 4th and 5th Fighter Aviation Corps of 2nd Air Army in the fighting over the troops.
cases.effect: The German XLVIII Panzer Corps chief of staff later described losses to Soviet aviation. His account corroborates exposure of German ground forces, but does not identify airframes destroyed at the seven airfields or tanks lost to particular sorties.
cases.limit: The Soviet airfield-destruction claim, the ground officer’s description, and the 1 July southern German/Hungarian deployment list refer to different targets and observations. No fleet-wide exchange ratio follows from them.

cases.title: Normandie’s escort and the ground front’s same-day return
cases.mission: GC 3 Normandie, one of four regiments in 303rd Fighter Aviation Division, recorded escorting Soviet Pe-2 bombers to Bogushevsk. Third Belorussian Front separately described 1st Air Army cover, reconnaissance and ground support that day.
cases.effect: The receiving front recorded 877 bombing and assault sorties, including 105 at night. Its return confirms support to its troops and distinguishes fighter cover from those 877 sorties.
cases.limit: No ground record identifies the result of this particular escorted formation’s bombing, and the other three regiments’ assignments do not prove that they flew with it.

cases.title: Bobruisk: an aircrew’s bridge report alongside the ground encirclement
cases.mission: On 27 June the 569th Assault Aviation Regiment attacked vehicles heading toward Titovka. Nine Pe-2s of the 24th Bomber Aviation Regiment were sent to the Berezina railway bridge at Bobruisk.
cases.effect: The Soviet report credits 569th Regiment with helping 9th Tank Corps and reports a bridge span falling during 24th Regiment’s mission. The lead bomber was lost and two crew died. Ninth Army’s own diary separately records overnight road interruptions and a badly hit signals centre at Osipovichi; a courier carried the morning order.
cases.limit: Ninth Army’s overnight entry precedes the daytime bridge attack. Its observable communications loss does not verify that particular bomb hit or explain the whole encirclement. The daytime bomber loss and the separate zero-loss evening strike concern different missions.

cases.title: What the 16th Air Army could field and what actually flew
cases.mission: The after-action report gives 3,037 serviceable aircraft before the offensive. The army records 2,531 aircraft flying 5,342 sorties on 16 April, including 1,188 day fighters on 2,545 sorties. Nineteen assigned regiments in three selected corps can be named.
cases.effect: The report attributes 6,548 sorties to the combined effort on this reporting front: 5,342 from 16th Air Army, 766 from 18th and 440 from 4th. The 17 April order names the 8th Guards Army’s sector as beneficiary of a further 6th Bomber Corps task.
cases.limit: The compilation counts 3,033 combat aircraft out of 3,188 total. Its 114 reconnaissance and spotting aircraft differ from 51 plus 67 in the army return. Separately, the primary transcription’s first-day sortie categories sum to 5,352 (109 + 1,315 + 1,383 + 2,545), ten above its twice-stated 5,342. Neither discrepancy has been silently corrected.

cases.title: Polish fighter cover along the northern advance
cases.mission: Poland’s 1st Fighter Regiment left Mirosławiec for Barnówko on 14 April. It reported twelve flights on 16 April, when its responsibilities included cover for 1st Army’s crossing of the Oder. The regiment also identifies escort of Polish 3rd Assault Regiment near Bad Freienwalde.
cases.effect: The ground history records 1st Army establishing a bridgehead over the Oder, reaching the Alte Oder on 18 April and crossing it after further fighting on 19 April. This supplies a dated ground sequence in the same sector.
cases.limit: The mapped Mirosławiec field was the departure base on 14 April. Barnówko was the operational base during the crossing; its surviving field description has not established a precise map point. The accounts do not isolate this escort’s effect on any individual crossing.

cases.title: How many of the 18th Air Army’s Berlin sorties reached the target?
cases.mission: The army’s overnight return lists 563 sorties for southwest Berlin. Of these, 517 aircraft reported bombing there: 139, 110, 201 and 60 from the four Guards Aviation Corps and seven from 45th Aviation Division.
cases.effect: Crews reported up to 30 fires and three large explosions. The first corps reported two Il-4s failing to return that night. The report also notes enemy fighter patrols and antiaircraft fire over Berlin.
cases.limit: The army’s total of 640 sorties includes Breslau and other tasks. Fires seen by crews cannot establish casualties, the effect on German units, or how the raid affected the following day’s Soviet ground advance. No German unit is identified as the patrol contact.

Allied.effort: 16th Army recorded 2,545 day-fighter sorties on 16 April. The 18th Army gives 563 Berlin sorties on 25/26 April and 517 bombers reporting over the target.
Allied.losses: The 16th Air Army’s 16 April account lists 87 aircraft lost, 75 on combat tasks and 12 on other flights. On 25/26 April the 18th Air Army’s first corps separately reported two Il-4s missing.
Allied.effect: The Polish ground account dates the Oder crossings. The 18th Air Army’s city raid produced crew-observed fires without independent building or ground-unit returns.

Axis.effort: Two JG 4 Gruppen have named 19 April stations. The Soviet night report observed patrols but could not identify their units.
Axis.losses: A German unit loss return matching the 25/26 April Soviet bombing report has not been identified.
Axis.effect: Soviet crews observed fires and a German air response. German records tying these to a local command’s ability to fight remain open.
